ai-d275be2a12.headline: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
ai-d275be2a12.fulltext:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.
A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO, the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “AI-pilled” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.
Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “Cracks in the AI Thesis”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.
“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.
Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.
“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”
The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.
“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”
“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.
Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct. Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.
“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

ai-ae94959362.headline: Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO hits resistance as investors balk at valuation
ai-ae94959362.fulltext:
Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO hits resistance as investors balk at valuation
Anthropic's IPO is in trouble as investors push back on the $1.5 trillion valuation and the tech market sells off. According to Reuters, potential backers doubt the planned roadshow can kick off next week as scheduled.
As recently as September, the company was eyeing a valuation of up to $2 trillion. Now some investors think even $1.5 trillion is too rich. One investor reportedly floated a valuation of just $1 trillion. Investors want a steeper discount because Anthropic is still losing money and burning through cash to scale its AI infrastructure. They're also waiting on October revenue numbers, which are missing from the updated S-1 filing.
The midterm elections made things worse. Ballot initiatives targeting data center expansion passed in several states, triggering the sharpest tech selloff in a year. The Wall Street Journal also reports that IPO investors are skeptical. If AI stocks stay under pressure, Anthropic could delay the offering, which some estimates peg at up to $100 billion in size. A delay could further shake confidence in the broader AI sector.

ai-453e1a62fd.headline: Lowdown: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines set out tiered framework, human oversight & incident reporting
ai-453e1a62fd.fulltext:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) released its Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines, outlining a risk-based framework for auditing AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated by organisations in India on November 4. The framework also covers AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users.
The guidelines set out requirements for governance, cybersecurity, data privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability, with audit obligations varying according to an AI system’s risk tier. They cover nine core audit domains and prescribe additional security requirements for generative AI, large language models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), agentic AI, multimodal AI and autonomous systems.
Core audit domains: The nine domains cover an AI system’s lifecycle, from design and procurement to deployment, monitoring and decommissioning.
AI Governance and Accountability: Organisations must establish governance structures, assign responsibilities, define accountability and maintain documentation for AI systems.
Data Lifecycle, Quality and Privacy: Audits must assess data collection, quality, integrity, privacy, access controls, retention and handling throughout the data lifecycle.
Model Risk Management: Auditors must examine model development, validation, performance, limitations, risks and controls.
AI Ethics, Bias and Fairness: Assessments must identify and address bias, discrimination and unfair outcomes.
Explainability and Transparency: Organisations must document AI system capabilities, limitations and decision-making processes, including applicable explainability measures.
Security, Adversarial Resilience and Incident Reporting: Audits must examine security controls, adversarial threats, vulnerabilities and incident response arrangements.
Continuous Monitoring, Drift Management and Validation: Organisations must monitor AI systems for performance degradation, data or model drift, and changes that require reassessment.
Human Oversight and Decision Accountability: Auditors must evaluate whether human oversight is appropriate to the system’s risk and whether decisions can be reviewed.
Third-Party and AI Supply-Chain Assurance: Organisations must assess risks arising from vendors, external models, dependencies and other components of the AI supply chain.
Risk tiers determine audit intensity: AI systems are classified into four risk tiers: Low, Moderate, High and Critical. The classification considers factors such as impact severity, decision-making autonomy, data sensitivity, scale and exposure, transparency, incident response readiness, reversibility, sector criticality, adversarial exposure and auditability. The assigned tier determines the depth, frequency and independence of audits, documentation requirements, human oversight and monitoring obligations.
Low risk: These systems have limited security, safety, operational or data risks. Their outputs are primarily advisory or assistive, with limited autonomy and no material impact on critical business processes. Audit requirements are comparatively streamlined.
Moderate risk: These systems influence business processes, service delivery or user interactions, with defined human oversight. A failure or compromise may cause recoverable operational, financial, data or service impact. The guidelines provide for annual independent audits by CERT-In-empanelled auditors.
High risk: These systems may have significant effects on operations, users, sensitive data or sectoral services. They require more rigorous and independent assessment, enhanced governance and stronger monitoring. The guidelines call for periodic independent audits, which may be conducted every six months where warranted.
Critical risk: These systems may pose severe or systemic risks, including significant consequences for critical infrastructure or safety. They require the highest level of audit scrutiny, including CERT-In-empanelled audits and continuous monitoring.
Risk-tier escalation may apply where the system’s use, impact or exposure changes, or where the assessment identifies factors warranting a higher classification.
Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): A human must approve or intervene in a decision before the AI system completes the relevant action.
Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL): A human supervises the AI system and can intervene, override, or stop its actions.
Human-over-the-Loop (HOVL): Human oversight takes place through monitoring, governance and periodic review, rather than direct intervention in every decision.
Auditors must assess whether the oversight model is appropriate to the system’s risk. This includes checking whether human reviewers have sufficient authority, competence, information and access to intervene effectively.
Contestability and decision review: Individuals affected by AI-assisted decisions must be able to seek review through contestability mechanisms, where applicable. Organisations must establish processes for human review, escalation and reconsideration. Auditors are expected to examine whether such mechanisms are documented and operational, and whether decisions can be reviewed by an authorised person.
Audit reporting, remediation and timelines: Audit findings are classified as Critical, High, Moderate or Low/Observation. Organisations must document findings, assign responsibility for remediation and track their closure.
Moderate findings: Organisations must submit a remediation plan within 30 business days and implement it within 60 days.
Critical, High and Moderate findings: Organisations must prepare Corrective Action Plans (CAPs).
A re-audit is required where an audit opinion is unsatisfactory, or where two or more Critical findings arise within three months. A re-audit may also be required sooner when directed by a regulator.
Audit requirements across the AI lifecycle: The audit methodology covers AI system design, procurement, data collection, development, training, validation, deployment, operation, retraining, monitoring and decommissioning.
The audit process includes engagement initiation, risk assessment, scoping, audit planning, evidence collection, technical testing, finding classification, reporting, remediation and follow-up verification. Organisations must identify the AI systems within their technical and organisational boundaries, classify them using the risk-tiering methodology and determine the applicable audit domains and evidence requirements.
Auditors must use the Core Audit Domains as the baseline and apply additional requirements for specialised AI systems wherever relevant. Applicable CERT-In requirements, sector-specific cybersecurity obligations, contractual requirements and other external obligations must be identified during scoping and incorporated into the audit criteria.
AI-assisted audit procedures may be used for evidence analysis, control mapping, technical testing and report preparation. However, such use must be subject to approved scope, confidentiality controls, tool validation, traceable evidence, and competent human review. AI-generated outputs cannot replace sufficient evidence or the auditor’s independent judgement.
Additional security requirements for advanced AI: Supplementary requirements apply to Generative AI, LLMs, RAG, Agentic AI, Multimodal AI, Multi-Agent AI and Autonomous or Cyber-Physical AI. These address risks that conventional cybersecurity controls may not adequately cover.
For generative AI and LLMs, auditors must consider prompt injection, sensitive-information disclosure, data and model poisoning, misinformation, hallucinations, and improper output handling. The guidelines also address deepfakes and require explicit consent in relevant contexts, alongside measures such as C2PA content provenance.
For RAG systems, assessments must examine the security of retrieval pipelines, vector databases, embeddings, access controls, and connected data sources. Agentic AI systems require scrutiny of tool use, excessive agency, least-privilege access, persistent memory, and unsafe autonomous actions.
Multimodal and multi-agent systems introduce additional risks involving cross-modal attacks, inter-agent communication, and the handling of data across different modalities. These architectures require appropriate security testing, including reassessment after material changes to the system.
Incident reporting and security obligations: Organisations must maintain processes to detect, respond to, and report AI-related security incidents, in accordance with applicable CERT-In requirements.
Incident response must be incorporated into AI security controls, including procedures for containment, investigation, recovery and post-incident review. Higher-risk systems must also maintain appropriate business continuity and resilience arrangements.

indian-startups-29404c9a8e.headline: Stockal’s US Trading Row: Missing Consent, A Chinese Microcap, And Unanswered Questions
indian-startups-29404c9a8e.fulltext: Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap. Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares. One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased. Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions. An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth. How The Trades Unfolded Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has raised over $15 Mn from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments. Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile. Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap. Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials. In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification. An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account. Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%. Differing Accounts Of Access In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions. Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.” Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation. Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far. This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts. Safeguards Under The Spotlight The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions. He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication. Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said. Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear. He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities. Borderless Sets Out Its Position Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts. It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts. The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators. Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed. Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Who Bears The Responsibility? The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024. HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities. While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses? Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability. For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

climate-energy-22e7bee5b2.headline: India approves Viability Gap Funding to support 92GWh of BESS and pumped hydro energy storage capacity
climate-energy-22e7bee5b2.fulltext:
India’s Union government has approved the next IR145 billion (US$1.5 billion) phase of the Viability Gap Funding (VGP) policy support mechanism for energy storage capacity additions.
In addition, a Ministry of Power official has reportedly said state power companies will likely soon be required to include energy storage in new renewable energy developments.
Announced earlier this week (4 November) by the office of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Press Information Bureau (PIB) of India following the Union Cabinet’s approval, the VGF scheme will offer Capex support to 92GWh of new energy storage deployments.
This will include 60GWh of pumped hydro energy storage (PHES), 30GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity and 2GWh of ‘alternative energy storage technologies.’
Together, the capacity will represent an estimated IR976 billion in energy storage investments, the government said. A domestic content requirement of 40% has also been introduced.
It follows the initial running of the scheme that saw the government offer support worth up to 40% of project Capex to 4GWh of projects for delivery in 2030-2031 after it was put forward in the 2023-2024 Union Budget.
It was later expanded to support 13.2GWh of new capacity, before its dramatic expansion with an additional IR54 billion to support 30GWh of battery storage was revealed in a Ministry of Power press conference in June 2025.
At the beginning of this year, the government issued a significant ruling on the VGF scheme, stipulating that developers must utilise a minimum of 20% domestic content, a requirement that has now been doubled.
Prime Minister Modi posted a tweet to X (formerly Twitter) describing the latest approval as a “massive” push to develop storage capacity, highlighting the 40% domestic content rule as a “unique feature.”
“Store More → Import Less → Power India Round the Clock!” the tweet read.
The scheme has been instrumental in supporting India’s emerging energy storage sector. As the name suggests, it is intended as a bridge to support the commercial viability of energy storage.
Many, including speakers at the recent Energy Storage Summit India 2026 in Greater Noida, have commented that VGF should therefore be a starting point as the industry matures, rather than a long-term crutch.
In an interview with Energy-Storage.news, Ateesh Samant, COO at independent power producer (IPP) Oyster Renewable, said that VGF “has been critical” in the early phase of the market, as was the waiver on Inter State Transmission System (ISTS) charges for co-located storage going online by mid-2028. Standalone BESS and PHES already receive waivers on those costs.
“The next step is to move from capital support to market design. That means markets that pay storage for the flexibility, capacity and grid services it provides,” Samant said, offering some recommendations such as increasing the spread between off-peak and peak electricity pricing.
At the India summit conference in October, Prashant Bhamu, deputy director of integrated resources planning at the Ministry of Power’s Central Electricity Authority (CEA) said India now has 5.3GWh of operational battery storage capacity and 185GWh under development.
CEA long-term resource adequacy planning indicates ~888GWh of energy storage capacity, including BESS and PHES, will be required by 2035-2036 across India, Bhamu said.
In other news, Ministry of Power secretary Pankaj Agarwal said recently that India will introduce mandatory energy storage capacity requirements for state utilities, Reuters news agency reported yesterday (5 November).
Speaking at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, the secretary also said more clean energy tenders related to energy storage will be forthcoming, although, according to Reuters, Agarwal added the situation was “fluid” regarding specific capacity addition requirements for state utilities.
India’s storage market is expanding, but project delivery depends on predictable procurement, domestic manufacturing and revenue models that support investment.

world-7fb3576e99.fulltext:

Related
- Tech layoffs were just the start: 1.6 million more US job cuts could push America toward recession

- Chip stocks bounce up to 8% as US stock futures recover after Thursday’s stock market crash - Jefferies says sell-off was ‘reactionary, not a reset’
Why Is TSM Stock Up Today
TSMC's American depositary receipts (ADRs) rose more than 6% in early trading. As investors reacting to the possibility that TSMC could expand beyond its core chipmaking business and enter a market dominated by Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology.
TSMC Considers Making 3D DRAM Chips for Nvidia
According to The Information report, TSMC has started drawing up plans to manufacture 3D dynamic random-access memory (DRAM). The proposal is reportedly linked to a request from Nvidia, which is TSMC's biggest customer.
The company is considering building new factories for memory production or acquiring an existing semiconductor facility and converting it for that purpose.
The reported effort is being led by Hsu Kuo-chin, a TSMC vice president responsible for advanced packaging operations who previously managed Micron's regional business.
AI Memory Shortage Puts TSMC in the Spotlight
The potential move comes as growing demand for AI hardware puts pressure on memory chip supplies. Nvidia and Apple are among the major technology companies seeking additional sources of memory.
3D DRAM uses vertically stacked memory cells rather than arranging them in a single horizontal layer. The design aims to increase memory capacity and represents a potential new direction for the industry.
TSMC's reported plans also come as Micron expands its own manufacturing capacity. In March, Micron agreed to acquire a Taiwan-based facility from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing for $1.8 billion, with plans to convert it for advanced memory production.
TSM Stock Could Enter Competition With Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron
Moving into advanced memory would put TSMC in direct competition with Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron, which already have established positions in the market.
TSMC has patents related to vertical DRAM technology, but moving from development to large-scale production could take years, The Information reported. The memory market also faces cycles of shortages and oversupply, which can affect chip prices and manufacturers' margins.
TSMC already has a working relationship with SK Hynix. In April 2024, the two companies signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on HBM4 development, with SK Hynix planning to use TSMC's advanced logic process to manufacture the memory chip's base die, according to SK Hynix.

work-careers-21158ad9b5.headline: India GCC tech hiring declines 3.5% in Q2, focus shifts to AI, data
work-careers-21158ad9b5.fulltext:
November 06, 2026 15:02 IST
4 Minutes Read
India's Global Capability Centres experienced a 3.5 per cent decline in tech hiring demand during Q2 FY27, even as the focus sharply shifted towards recruiting professionals in high-demand areas like Artificial Intelligence, data analytics, and cybersecurity.
- Tech hiring demand at India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) fell 3.5 per cent sequentially in Q2 FY27.
- Manufacturing and industrial, and BFSI sectors experienced significant declines in hiring demand.
- Demand for AI, data analytics, and cybersecurity professionals surged, with AI and data roles growing 14 per cent quarter-on-quarter.
- Tier-II cities saw a 13 per cent growth in hiring demand, with Coimbatore leading the increase.
- Talent shortages remain acute for specialised digital skills, particularly in AI, data, and cybersecurity.
Tech hiring demand at India's global capability centres (GCCs) fell 3.5 per cent sequentially during the July-September quarter of FY27.
This indicates a slowdown in fresh recruitment compared with the previous quarter, according to a report by staffing firm Quess Corp, released on Thursday.
The report titled, India GCC Tech Talent Landscape Q2 FY27, showed that manufacturing and industrial, the largest sector by hiring share, saw demand fall of 9 per cent.
And, banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) recorded an 8 per cent decline.
Software and digital engineering roles saw an 11 per cent decline in demand growth, while information technology (IT) service management and digital operations witnessed a 10 per cent fall.
The telecom and networks sector witnessed the sharpest fall, at 24 per cent, while professional services and consulting saw a 2 per cent dip.
"Q2FY27 was a recalibration quarter for India's GCCs. Hiring demand changed by -3.5 per cent quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q), but the skills mix moved firmly towards artificial intelligence (AI), data and cyber resilience.
"Global parents are asking their India centres to own outcomes, not just add capacity, and headcount plans now follow that mandate," the report said.
Meanwhile, demand for AI, data analytics and cybersecurity professionals continued to rise. Demand for AI, data and analytics roles grew 14 per cent Q-o-Q, the fastest among job categories, while cybersecurity and risk management hiring increased 12 per cent.

The AI developer has been in talks for more than a month to raise a large funding round after delaying its plans for an initial public offering. Softbank, Founders Fund and T. Rowe Price declined to comment. Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
The reduced funding goals represent a stark shift for a fundraising juggernaut that helped usher in the current AI boom. The sentiment around AI has also changed dramatically since the round kicked off, due to concerns about the spending spree on physical infrastructure for artificial intelligence and the potential for new roadblocks to data center construction following the US midterm elections.

ai-c71b99d867.headline: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small claims top spot among western open-weight models
ai-c71b99d867.fulltext:
Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small claims top spot among western open-weight models
Key Points
- Thinking Machines, the startup from former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is releasing Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion parameters, 17 billion of which are active at any given time.
- On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Inkling 2 Small scores 31, an 18-point jump over its predecessor and roughly on par with Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash, with especially strong gains in agentic tasks.
- The improved performance comes at a price, though. The model generates more output tokens and costs six times as much per task as its predecessor. It's initially available as a proprietary offering through the Tinker platform, with weights under an Apache license to follow.
Inkling 2 Small claims to be the strongest Western open-weight model, with 17 billion active parameters and benchmark scores that far exceed its predecessor.
The startup from former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, Thinking Machines, has unveiled Inkling 2 Small, its second model generation. Inkling models are designed as base models for fine-tuning, which could make them especially attractive for specialized applications.
The mixture-of-experts model contains a total of 594 billion parameters, of which 17 billion are active at any given time. It accepts text and images as input and offers an adjustable thinking depth that lets users choose between speed and thoroughness.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Inkling 2 Small scores 31, according to Thinking Machines. That's 18 points above the predecessor Inkling Small (13) and roughly on par with Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash.
The biggest gains show up in agentic tasks, where the model independently executes multi-step workflows. On AutomationBench-AA the score jumps from 5 to 46 percent, and on FrontierCode 2.0 it rises from 5 to 25 percent. On the knowledge-work benchmark AA-Briefcase, Inkling 2 Small hits 1,527 Elo, 615 points above its predecessor. The hallucination rate drops from 61 to 27 percent, but largely because the model answers fewer questions. The response rate falls from 77 to 53 percent.
Costs rise but stay well below the competition
The better results come partly at the cost of higher token usage. Inkling 2 Small produces roughly 150,000 output tokens per task on average, about four times as many as its predecessor. At $1.18 per task it costs nearly six times as much, according to Artificial Analysis. That's still far cheaper than Gemini 3.8 Flash ($7.77) or Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($10.02), and it lands closer to the price range of low-cost Chinese models.
Thinking Machines says it trained the model with reinforcement learning on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks. An automated evaluation system checked whether the code worked and how the model approached each task. On FrontierCode 2.0, Inkling 2 Small reaches 25.4 percent, on DeepSWE 72.1 percent, and on SWEBench Pro v2 (Hard) 86.3 percent. The new Deepseek-V4.1-Flash still leads on most of those tests, hitting 28.5 percent on FrontierCode and 77 percent on DeepSWE.
Vision and design scores lead among open-weight models
Thinking Machines says the model is strongest in text recognition, infographic interpretation, and visual reasoning. On the document benchmark GDP.pdf, which tests whether models can answer questions from complex PDF documents, it scores 25.2 percent, the highest among the compared models. On MMMU Pro, a benchmark for multimodal understanding of academic tasks involving diagrams and figures, Inkling 2 Small reaches 81.6 percent.
On PerceptionBench, which tests the visual perception ability of multimodal models, it leads with 64.7 percent. For visual creation, the model earns a 1,340 Elo rating on DesignArena Website, where users rate AI-generated websites in head-to-head comparisons. That's the highest score among open-weight models. Thinking Machines says the model has also made progress in 3D modeling.
In a somewhat unusual demonstration, the team pitted the model against its own researchers in a blind wine tasting. Working from a photo alone, Inkling 2 Small correctly identified three wines in 19 out of 20 attempts.
Compact training run, open weights coming soon
The total training run is remarkably compact compared with the competition. Across all phases the model processed about 12 trillion tokens, according to Thinking Machines, far fewer than comparable rivals. The reinforcement-learning phase after base training needed only 3 trillion tokens on 2,048 GPUs over nine days.
Thinking Machines says the model sometimes communicates inefficiently, and that's likely a bigger issue, it doesn't always pick the best tools for large codebases. It doesn't support audio and is less optimized for chat. It can also overreact to health-related topics and produce cluttered output.
For now, Thinking Machines offers the model through its Tinker platform. The company plans to release the weights under an Apache 2.0 license once external safety testing wraps up. That's one of the most permissive open-source licenses and an advantage over more restrictive open-weight licenses such as those from Meta or Mistral. Thinking Machines says the model belongs to a family of different sizes, and the company plans to release more variants soon.

ai-a66e37d5ba.headline: RBI meets bankers amidst rising AI cyber-attacks, mandates security audits
ai-a66e37d5ba.fulltext:
Amidst the rising AI-assisted cyberattacks, especially on the financial sector, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), India’s central bank and main regulator for the banking sector, has possibly for the first time met bankers to address this issue since Cert-In started publishing advisories regarding the vulnerabilities reported.
According to an exclusive report by Head and Tale’s Arti Singh, the RBI reportedly held a nearly two-hour meeting with banks on Wednesday and issued a “confidential advisory” dated November 3. The banker told the reporter that the regulator “gave banks a dressing down” and stressed that banks are responsible for securing these arrangements. The banker also stated that individual frauds ranged from Rs. 3 crore to Rs. 15 crore, adding that the number of cyberattack attempts worried banks more.
The confidential RBI advisory reportedly also asked NBFCs which use APIs for a security audit by CERT-In empaneled auditor. These are the independent auditing companies which are approved by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). A full list of cybersecurity organizations which are listed on CERT-In’s website can be accessed here.
CERT-In names a threat actor: CERT-In’s November 4 advisory named a threat actor, “CRAFTY FALCON”. It said attackers used Rs. 1 transfers to test fund flows before larger transactions. It also said they bypassed IP allow-listing by routing traffic through shared third-party IP pools. CERT-In recommended beneficiary cooling periods and maker-checker approval for merchant settlements. Similarly, CERT-In has issued similar notices, you can find them here and here.
The next day, after the RBI meeting on November 3, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), which works under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), issued a public advisory on AI-assisted attacks on banks, NBFCs and fintechs. Both concern the application programming interfaces (APIs) that lenders use to disburse money.
Similarly, on the same day, CERT-In released AI Security Auditing Guidelines. Read MediaNama’s lowdown of the guidelines here.
Maintain a full API client inventory. The regulator has asked banks to capture business profile, services used, account and integration details, transaction limits, and key business, technical and security contacts.
Require CERT-In audits for NBFC clients. RBI has said the audit must be completed before onboarding new NBFCs, while existing clients have until February 3, 2027.
Conduct audits at least once a year. The regulator has reportedly asked banks to repeat the audit after any material cyber incident and to track completion and act on non-compliance.
Risk-assess non-NBFC API clients immediately. RBI also asked banks to require a periodic audit within three months for BCs, PAs, PSPs and fintechs, sooner if risk is higher.
Brief all API clients every three months on the current threat landscape, as per the regulator’s advisory.
Bring API transactions under fraud-risk and monitoring frameworks. The regulator has asked banks to set thresholds and behavioural baselines per client.
Flag material deviations. RBI has said banks must watch for volume or value spikes, transactions just below limits, odd-hour or holiday activity, bursts of new beneficiaries, mule patterns, failed log-ins and invalid API requests.
Monitor changes in apps. The regulator has asked banks to watch for changes in user-agent, app version, OS and network attributes, with technical changes due by December 3.
Secure banks’ own API infrastructure. The regulator has said banks must cover access management, network segmentation, patching and monitoring, as attackers may pivot through a compromised client.
Enforce beneficiary whitelisting. RBI has also asked banks to pre-register verified end-customer accounts per client, reject unregistered payouts, and allow additions or modifications only via a separate MFA-protected channel.
Enforce maker-checker or out-of-band confirmation. The regulator has said banks must add extra authorisation for API debit requests via a separate channel, applying it to all transactions or those above a risk-based threshold.
Require at least one safeguard from regulated entities using API-based fund transfers. The regulator has said new integrations must comply before they go-live, while existing ones have time until December 3, 2026.
Make debit information available quickly so clients can reconcile transactions one by one, as per the regulator’s direction.
Allow narrow, case-by-case exceptions only for highly automated payments where neither control is practical. The regulator has said a written application and documented risk assessment are required.
Set per-transaction and daily cumulative limits effective immediately. The regulator has asked banks to calibrate them to declare and observe business profile and risk.
Implement intra-day or velocity limits within one month to prevent bursts of transactions. RBI has said material limit increases need a documented risk assessment.
Treat maker-checker as a compensating safeguard for intra-day limits if commensurate with risk and documented, as the regulator has allowed.
Enforce immediate incident reporting and recovery. It has asked banks to ensure clients promptly report any actual or suspected compromise of systems connected to API-based payments.
CERT-In Director General Dr Sanjay Bahl, in written answers to MediaNama on November 2 and 3, described what worries the agency. He said that “delegated authority without commensurate guardrails and that AI agents are being trusted faster than they are being secured” concerns India’s nodal cyber security agency.
Note: MediaNama’s interview predates the RBI’s confidential advisory becoming public. Read the full interview here.
“What would change is the speed, scale and level of automation at which cyber activities take place. Defensive capabilities would therefore need to evolve accordingly from human-speed monitoring and manual containment to continuous, automated machine-speed defence.” – CERT-In Director General, Dr Sanjay Bahl.
AU Small Finance Bank is probing a “potential data leak” on a Salesforce-hosted platform after hackers claimed a breach. The bank says its systems are unaffected.
CoinDCX first dismissed reports of a breach, then confirmed a loss of about Rs. 152 crore.
Central Bank of India alleges hackers siphoned off Rs. 13.97 crore through its financial messaging system. It says it could not trace 187 transfers.
SBI confirmed a suspected breach of 3,897 customer records. Later they revealed that the customers have been informed through email and/or WhatsApp.
CBFC reportedly exposed scripts, distribution deals and censorship records for over 500 films. The board says it found no trace of the documents.
Amagi Media Labs faced an extortion attempt from a hacker claiming to hold operational and network data.
eMudhra is exiting the SSL/TLS certificate business days after researchers exposed weak private keys in eight intermediate certificates.
Railway, a cloud hosting platform, asked users to replace API keys after a cyberattack potentially exposed customer secrets.
CERT-In disclosed that AI agents accessed live Indian systems without authorisation during research and evaluation.
Anthropic said its Claude model found vulnerabilities across five targets, including Chrome, Android, Windows and Linux. It has not disclosed its success rate or computing costs.

ai-35bf191231.headline: TRAI recommends India-based network control, traffic monitoring for satellite providers
ai-35bf191231.fulltext:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on November 5, 2026, released recommendations on a framework for Satellite Communication Network (SCN) provider authorisation and spectrum assignment. The recommendations propose a new authorisation category for satellite network providers, who would supply network capacity to eligible telecom service providers rather than directly serve users. Alongside the proposed framework, TRAI has set out security conditions governing network control, monitoring, gateway infrastructure and the use of satellite networks for cross-border services.
Network Control Facilities Must Be Located in India: TRAI has recommended that the operation, maintenance and control facilities for an SCN provider’s satellite communication network be located in India. The requirement would also cover user terminals belonging to partnering authorised entities that connect to the provider’s network.
SCN providers must ensure that their networks are used only to deliver telecommunications services for which the partnering entity holds authorisation. They must also prevent their networks from being used for unauthorised activities, including surveillance and electronic warfare, or in a manner that could prejudice India’s sovereignty and security.
The recommendations further require SCN providers to report to the Central Government any attempt to access or use their satellite networks through a user terminal that is not registered with the partnering entity. The report must include information about the terminal and its location.
To meet this requirement, providers must undertake the technical measures necessary to identify and report such attempts. However, TRAI has not prescribed a specific technology, protocol or authentication mechanism for detecting unregistered terminals.
Government Can Direct Security Measures For Satellite Gateways: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers submit the location and technical details of each satellite earth station gateway to the Central Government or a designated agency before establishing it. The government or agency may examine the submitted information and direct the provider to take specific actions in relation to the gateway’s establishment.
The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests, as well as implement mitigation measures, as directed by the government. These provisions would give the government a role in reviewing gateway infrastructure before it is set up and in requiring operational measures where necessary.
Separately, TRAI has recommended that SCN providers offer a real-time traffic monitoring facility to ensure compliance with requirements governing Indian user traffic. This includes restrictions on routing traffic through foreign gateways and on mirroring Indian traffic to foreign satellite or telecom networks.
The recommendations also state that user terminals connected to a partnering authorised entity must not communicate directly through satellites without routing via a satellite earth station gateway. These conditions form part of the technical and operating obligations proposed for SCN provider authorisation.
Direct Terminal Communication And Interference: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers prevent direct communication between two or more user terminals through one or more satellites unless the traffic passes through a satellite earth station gateway. This would apply to terminals connected to partnering authorised entities.
The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests whenever the Central Government requires them to. Providers must take all necessary measures directed by the government to mitigate interference.
These conditions would place responsibility on SCN providers to ensure that satellite network traffic follows the prescribed gateway architecture and that interference can be monitored and addressed through measures mandated by the government.

deep-tech-41b86daadd.headline: Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics
deep-tech-41b86daadd.fulltext:
Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas.
ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China. The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.”
Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI. For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals.
In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs.
Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated, with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co.
ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI
ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation, software, force- and power-limited cobots, and AMRs. The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive, electronics, and logistics.
ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion.
“Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis. “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.”
“Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report. She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes.
“AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little, a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn. “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.”
“SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.”
Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern
“Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models.
“The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X.
Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI.
“What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report.
“China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.”
Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics, posted to LinkedIn: “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.”
“I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?”
“My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not that great to begin with fall even further.”
“There may still be negotiations that find a way forward,” concluded Little. “For now, ABB is in a pickle.”

deep-tech-d9c54b5db0.headline: CesiumAstro Raises $730M, Reaches Valuation Above $4.5B
deep-tech-d9c54b5db0.fulltext:
MERRITT ISLAND, FL—CesiumAstro plans to build and deploy a new constellation—called Synchronicity—consisting of 737 satellites. The company made a downpayment on it Thursday, closing a $730M financing round.
Janus Henderson led the equity round, which included additional participation from Insight Partners, Sands Capital, Sumitomo Corporation of Americas, Woven Capital, Incharge Capital, Magnetar, AV, and NewSpace Capital.
The round included a $100M debt facility provided by the Export-Import Bank of the United States and JPMorgan in addition to $630M in equity financing.
Small step, giant leap: The announcement comes just over a month after CesiumAstro sent its first satellite to orbit. Element-1 launched on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare in October, on a mission designed to pave the way for the full Synchronicity constellation.
“You can build a satellite like you used to that’s a billion dollars and bullet proof, but you’ve taken a decade to test it out,” CesiumAstro founder and CEO Shey Sabripour told Payload. “We did [this satellite] in two and a half years.”
Element-1 is the first of eight planned spacecraft with launches secured between 2028 and 2029. These sats are intended to build out CesiumAstro’s in-space compute capabilities.
The proposed Synchronicity fleet is designed to broadcast over Ku-, Ka-, and V-band frequencies, and will come equipped with onboard compute capabilities to deliver competitive flexibility and resiliency for commercial and national security customers.
How the hundreds of Synchronicity sats will get to orbit, however, is an open question. Sabripour said CesiumAstro is strategizing about what partnerships are necessary to reach its goal of 350 satellites in orbit by 2032.
All for one: The constellation will combine tech that CesiumAstro has spent nearly a decade building, through in-house R&D and a slew of recent acquisitions.
In the past year, CesiumAstro purchased three companies, each adding critical IP to CesiumAstro’s portfolio.
- Jariet Technologies, an RF System-on-Chip semiconductor company focused on satcom, electronic warfare, and radar tech. The acquisition added “advanced mixed-signal semiconductors, digital signal processing, and digital beamforming capabilities” to Cesium’s arsenal, according to the announcement.
- 1Aardvark, a mission software company, giving Cesium spacecraft the ability to operate “in contested or connectivity-constrained environments.”
- Vidrovr, an AI company focused on signal analysis, accelerating CesiumAstro’s integration of AI into its satcom operations.
And CesiumAstro doesn’t plan on stopping the shopping spree anytime soon.
“There’s a few things that we’re still buying and will continue to buy if the supply chain is resilient and made in the US,” Sabripour said. “If it’s not, and it’s being endangered because there are a lot of acquisitions then we’ll buy them. We have our eyes on quite a few.”
In addition to more potential M&A opportunities, CesiumAstro plans to use the new funds to invest heavily in its manufacturing capacity—announcing plans to spent $500M over the next five years to expand its footprint in Austin and purchase 270,000 sq ft of manufacturing space.
Although the company’s acquisitions have brought on hundreds of new employees since the buying spree began in February, it plans to add 550 more jobs by 2030.

         TAIPEI
     A global race to build AI infrastructure is unleashing billions of dollars of investment in advanced chip packaging, a once unglamorous aspect of technology that has become a critical bottleneck in turning out the world's most powerful processors.
As demand for artificial intelligence chips outstrips available packaging capacity, companies from Nvidia and AMD to lesser-known players in Taiwan are expanding production, while equipment makers develop new tools, interviews with more than a dozen industry executives and analysts show.
"Packaging was always that thing that you just didn't worry about," former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger, now a partner at Playground Global, told reporters in Taipei recently.
Advanced packaging could eventually account for as much as half the value of a chip product, Gelsinger estimated, as some of today's graphics and central processing units can integrate 10 or more chips, sometimes as many as 20.
Revenue from advanced packaging is forecast to overtake that earned via the traditional route for the first time in 2026, says research firm Yole Group, with capital spending on the technology expected to near $28 billion.
The world's largest contract chipmaker, Taiwan's TSMC , dominates the most sophisticated advanced packaging technology, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS.
The technology links separate pieces of silicon, such as processors and memory chips, on a shared base, to let them work together at high speed.
It is widely used by Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, as well as cloud companies developing their own AI chips.
But TSMC's capacity limits have spurred some chip designers to seek additional supply.
Nvidia, for example, is providing billions of dollars in financing to expand CoWoS packaging capacity at Siliconware Precision Industries, or SPIL, a unit of Taiwan's ASE Technology , said an industry executive familiar with the matter, who sought anonymity for lack of authorisation to talk to media.
The funding will support new factory space and equipment, the executive said. The scale of the support has not previously been reported.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. ASE said it does not comment on market rumours involving its customers.
The scramble to invest reflects a broader change in manufacturing of powerful chips, as more chip designers use advanced packaging to integrate multiple chips, such as processors and memory, into a single package.
That allows the ensemble to work together faster as one system, in contrast with the practice of decades, when packaging served mainly to protect chips and provide the electrical connections to attach them to circuit boards.
The shift comes as it become harder and costlier to win performance gains by shrinking and adding transistors, the tiny switches inside a chip.
The newer packaging technique is especially important for AI chips, which need to shuffle vast amounts of data between processors and nearby memory. Speeding up such transfers hastens the process of training and running AI models.
TSMC's tight capacity offers an opportunity for smaller suppliers, such as Taiwan's Powertech Technology.
"Everyone is looking for a solution outside TSMC," its chairman, D K Tsai, told reporters in August. "They don't want to rely entirely on TSMC."
Powertech, also known as PTI, is betting on panel-level packaging, which uses larger rectangular panels instead of round wafers as the chip packaging platform.
This way, it can accommodate more chips in each production run and waste less material, an advantage as AI processors become larger and more complex.
PTI is working with AMD and Broadcom on the technology as the industry seeks to demonstrate its viability for larger, more complex chip packages used in AI and high-performance computing.
"The most important thing right now is capacity," said PTI Senior Vice President Jim Lin, adding that customers were waiting for the company to ramp up production.
Powertech plans to invest $400 million in an advanced packaging joint venture with Broadcom in Singapore. Production could begin in 2028, Tsai said.
To support larger and more complex chip packages, TSMC is developing its own panel-based technology, called chip-on-panel-on-substrate, or CoPoS.
In April, it said it had built a pilot line and expected production to begin within a couple of years, but CoWoS remains TSMC's main AI-packaging technology.
AMD has also unveiled investments of more than $10 billion across Taiwan's semiconductor industry, including partnerships with ASE, SPIL and Powertech on advanced packaging.
Asked if Powertech's panel-level packaging technology could offer an alternative to TSMC's technology, AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su did not directly address the question but acknowledged the need for more advanced packaging capacity.
"I think CoWoS and advanced packaging are super important for our high-performance computing going forward," Su told Reuters in Taipei in October.
"TSMC has been an incredible partner in advanced packaging, and we're going to continue to do more together. And yes, we do need more capacity overall."
Panel-level packaging would reduce material waste when packaging larger AI chips, said Microsoft Azure hardware chief Rani Borkar, though the company has not decided whether or when it will adopt the technology.
The packaging boom is also opening a new market for makers of semiconductor equipment.
Such companies have traditionally focused on earlier stages of chipmaking, when circuitry is built onto silicon. Advanced packaging comes later, when chips, memory or other components are joined into a finished high-performance unit.
Advanced packaging was growing much faster than the market for chip-making gear, though it remained smaller, said Seiji Nakama, president of Tokyo Electron Taiwan.
The market for advanced packaging, including panel-level technology, could grow significantly within three to five years, said an official of US equipment maker Applied Materials.
"It's near-term," said Sree Kesapragada, a vice president at the company, which is increasingly focusing on the new format. "It's not like, 10 years, 15 years off."
