climate-energy-4f5a31921c.headline: China’s Proposed Tech Export Curbs Test India’s Solar Manufacturing Push
climate-energy-4f5a31921c.fulltext:
[Text below is Frontline Magazine's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
China’s proposed curbs on solar technology exports have once again exposed the vulnerabilities in India’s plans to ramp up domestic solar manufacturing.
Exclusive reporting, market intelligence, and insider access that shapes billion-dollar decisions in renewable energy and clean technology.
In March, Belgium Prime Minister Bart De Wever wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with a stark warning: China was devastating Europe’s economy. The bloc had reached a point of no return, and this required a tougher collective response even at the cost of Chinese retaliation. In response, a Global Times editorial accused De Wever of digging a hole for the EU and scapegoating China for Europe’s own “long-accumulated structural issues”, including weak growth, high energy costs, and sluggish innovation. Both sides had a point: China Shock 2.0 is real and greatly distorts the global economy as the country exports its macroeconomic imbalances, yet the response to it is being shaped as much by geopolitics, and by genuine failures at the receiving end, as by the economics of the shock itself.
The original China Shock was a story of labour-cost arbitrage following China’s 2001 WTO accession: cheap, abundant labour pulling Western assembly work into Chinese factories, hollowing out manufacturing towns but leaving developing countries room to climb the ladder below China. China Shock 2.0 is different in its nature, driven by state-backed dominance in innovation-intensive, capital-deep sectors such as electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar photovoltaics, legacy-node semiconductors, robotics, and increasingly frontier artificial intelligence and advanced pharmaceuticals where China is overtaking incumbents. The 2026 ASPI Critical Technology Tracker finds China leading in 69 of 74 tracked technologies against just 5 for the US.
China’s manufacturing footprint accounts for roughly a third of global manufacturing value-added. In 2025, China had a global trade surplus of $1.197 trillion, with the manufactured-goods surplus approaching $2 trillion. This emerged despite US tariffs that briefly touched 125 per cent before the Busan de-escalation; exporters redirected towards the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the EU, the Gulf, and the Global South.
A $19 trillion economy confronting weak domestic demand, a deflating property sector, and demographic headwinds is exporting its way out of a serious predicament. China’s political economy militates against currency appreciation or a structural shift towards domestic consumption that would narrow the surplus.
The IMF estimates the fiscal cost of China’s industrial policy at approximately 4.4 per cent of the GDP annually through just four channels—cash subsidies, tax benefits, subsidised credit, and subsidised land—with total support potentially reaching 7 to 8 per cent of the GDP. Combined with predatory pricing and loss-making “zombie firms” kept alive by local financing, this discourages manufacturing capability elsewhere, contributing to premature deindustrialisation and retarded industrialisation happening at once, at opposite ends of the global income ladder.
A conversation in Beijing
At a prestigious Beijing forum two years ago, I argued that concerns about Chinese excess capacity extended well beyond developed economies to developing countries like India. I was accused of parroting Western propaganda. Last year, I had the quiet satisfaction of noting that Chinese President Xi Jinping himself had apparently fallen for that same propaganda, given his explicit references to China’s “involution” problem, meaning zero-sum price wars among Chinese firms suffering from excess capacities. Beijing’s official position, epitomised by a Xinhua-backed commentary dismissing the “China Shock 2.0” narrative as a Western “concoction”, coexists uneasily with Xi’s calls for the “orderly exit” of outdated capacity and curbs on “disorderly” price competition.
China is not winning its battle against involution. The clearest case is the failed polysilicon cartel: six leading producers proposed raising 50 billion Chinese yuan to buy out and idle a third of the country’s polysilicon capacity, only for the regulator to block the plan on monopoly grounds. This protected downstream consumers but left chronic losses and overcapacity unresolved, showing how local-government incentives and youth unemployment make capacity reduction politically difficult.
By late 2025, every one of China’s 8 largest solar panel and wafer manufacturers was loss-making. The picture in EVs is scarcely better: of the roughly 60 domestic EV brands competing for market share, only 3—BYD, Xiaomi, and Leapmotor—turned a profit. In other words, China’s commanding presence in global green-technology markets has not translated into commercial viability. The persistence of large-scale losses despite rising exports underscores the extent to which China’s industrial strategy relies on state-directed capital rather than market discipline, raising further questions about the country’s claims of operating as a market economy.
What we are witnessing is the global manifestation of a deeper China Syndrome: an entrenched set of internal compulsions that ensure the shock is not episodic but structural, chronic, and strategically consequential. Zhang Bin of the China Finance 40 Forum, formerly of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, makes the same case from inside China: insufficient domestic demand pushes firms to export and “go global”, swelling the surplus and, in his words, “provoking trading partners’ dissatisfaction”.
Chinese economists argue, not without merit, that much of the surge reflects genuine competitiveness: scale, vertical integration, innovation, and process mastery that Western and Global South supply chains cannot replicate. However, China has a problem with its macroeconomic model: forced savings, a structurally undervalued renminbi, and an addiction to export-led growth.
Deindustrialisation, North and South
The resultant destabilisation cuts across the rich-poor divide. Germany is the starkest developed-economy case, its car exports to China down sharply since 2022 and its once-formidable China trade surplus swinging into deficit. German economic institutes estimate that intensified import competition from China has cost Germany between 2,50,000 and 4,00,000 industrial jobs since 2019, with current losses running at roughly 15,000 industrial jobs per month in 2025–26.
But the pressure is not confined to advanced economies: China has not vacated the labour-intensive sectors of the first shock even as it seizes advanced sectors, closing the route by which industrialisation cascades to developing economies.
The analysis cannot stop at economics; it must be situated in a changed geopolitical context that has made collective resistance more necessary and more difficult. Trade defence and industrial revival measures—including anti-dumping duties, rules of origin, the US CHIPS and Inflation Reduction Acts, and an emerging EU instrument modelled on America’s Section 301—have proved insufficient. The US tariffs of 47.5 per cent on Chinese exports, even after the Busan understanding of October 2025, have not slowed the global export surge; exporters redirect towards markets with softer defences. The US’ posture has been erratic and transactional, drifting from strategic competition towards managed accommodation with China: Busan delivered tactical de-escalation on tariffs and rare earths without touching China’s industrial policy architecture.
Europe, meanwhile, is fractured by a triple whammy: the loss of cheap Russian energy, the dilution of American security guarantees, and China’s export surge hitting automotive, machinery and green-technology industries. De Wever’s letter is a symptom of this fracture, not a solution: individual countries, Hungary among them, keep cutting bilateral deals with Chinese battery and EV manufacturers that Brussels cannot police. China has skilfully exploited this, positioning itself as the predictable, rules-respecting power against an erratic US.
The developing world’s failure has different roots but a similar outcome. Mexico, Indonesia, and Brazil have imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, yet the systemic pressure continues unabated: no single developing economy has the market size to alter Chinese exporters’ calculus, and there is no Global South equivalent to the EU’s collective machinery, so China can play them off against one another. A deeper bind compounds this: developing economies need China’s cheap solar panels, batteries, and grid equipment to keep their energy transitions affordable, even as those imports displace the manufacturing jobs their industrial strategies depend on, and few have the fiscal space to subsidise domestic producers at Chinese scale or cushion displaced workers as advanced welfare states can.
What this means for India
India’s China shock is no less real but far less visible in aggregate numbers: there is no single national estimate of jobs lost to Chinese imports, only scattered district-level studies on micro, small, and medium enterprises and anecdotal evidence from manufacturing clusters pointing to significant impact. China accounts for nearly 17 per cent of India’s total imports, with heavy dependence in pharmaceutical ingredients, electronics, solar components, industrial machinery, and rare-earth magnets. Bilateral trade touched a record $155.6 billion in 2025, with China’s surplus against India reaching $116 billion, roughly a tenth of China’s global surplus, as China overtook the US as India’s largest trading partner. There is a deliberate pincer: export curbs deny India the battery and EV technology needed to reduce dependence, while WTO challenges to India’s solar and EV subsidies attack the local-content rules meant to build that independence—leverage applied at both ends of the same chain.
The security dimension compounds the economic one. India’s exclusion of Chinese vendors from its 5G rollout in 2021 was an early, sound decision against what Anatoly Motkin has called China’s “Silicon Curtain”, the embedding of Chinese digital infrastructure abroad through below-market pricing and hardware lock-ins. The problem is compounded by the live and militarised border, China’s deepening nexus with Pakistan, and the risk of a “G2 overlay”, tacit US-China coordination that could leave India reacting to bargains it had no part in shaping. Yet India, while vocal about unfair trade practices, oscillates between liberalisation impulses and defensive measures, reverting to the slogan of India and China being “partners and development opportunities for each other” without getting satisfaction on its trade concerns. There is growing pressure on the government from corporate houses to return to business as usual with China.
India’s engagement with China has produced a limited, carefully qualified thaw since the Kazan and Tianjin summits. Press Note 2 of 2026 clarified the land-border investment restrictions of 2020’s Press Note 3, permitting expedited approval of Chinese minority investment in sectors covering some 58 per cent by value of India’s imports from China. However, China’s cumulative investment in India between 2000 and 2025 stood at just $2.5 billion, against roughly $175 billion in Chinese outward investment in 2025 alone, and China has shown itself more inclined to slow India’s manufacturing ambitions, through mineral export curbs and informal delays on equipment exports, than to accelerate them.
India’s own response is a mixed story. The mobile-phone production-linked incentive (PLI) policy, rewarding manufactured output and escalating domestic content over time, is a template that can be replicated in solar modules, battery chemistry, and active pharmaceutical ingredients. But India’s solar sector shows the trap as much as the promise: a new ingot-wafer facility launched this April in Visakhapatnam is a genuine move up the value chain, yet it still depends on Chinese-dominated polysilicon, cell-manufacturing equipment, and rare-earth magnets. Dependency is being relocated rather than removed.

By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump named trusted aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress. 
Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.
A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party’s defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.
In a social media post, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors,” and he praised Wiles for doing “an outstanding job.” Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.
A White House official said Miller’s appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.
“He’s not changing course,” the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters this week repudiating Trump’s domestic agenda and foreign policy.
While Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill, the elevation of Miller, known for being uncompromising, could suggest a more confrontational approach and push to advance the president’s agenda, several White House officials said.
Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday’s election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be “more aggressive” as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.
MILLER DROVE IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN
Miller, 41, is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides and is one of few who served throughout his first and second terms in office.
Since Trump’s return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump’s domestic agenda and has had the president’s ear.
He is perhaps best known for driving Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a target of 3,000 arrests a day. In pursuit of that target, federal immigration agents expanded their list of targets to include migrants who had been living in the US for decades.
He was also deeply involved in Trump’s campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration’s battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions.
Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement of Miller’s promotion by calling him a “reckless extremist” in a posting on X.
SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION SETBACK
The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president’s gatekeeper. The person manages White House staff, organizes the president’s time and schedule, and maintains contact with other government departments and lawmakers.
Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump’s political operation, according to a White House official.
The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff.
She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump’s prior top aides. She maintained her role even while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer.
Wiles rarely challenged Trump’s policies but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role.
Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president.

Strategic HR
ServiceNow layoffs hit UK, US and India as company restructures workforce
Employees in India, the UK and the US are affected as ServiceNow continues its AI-led restructuring, with severance costs rising sharply in 2026.
ServiceNow has launched another round of global layoffs, with employees in India, the UK and the US affected, according to CTech. The company has not disclosed the number of roles being eliminated as it reshapes operations around efficiency and artificial intelligence.
The latest cuts come as the enterprise software company pursues a workforce strategy focused on AI-driven efficiencies and investment in specialised skills. ServiceNow said it was making structural changes while maintaining its previously stated goal of ending 2026 with the same overall headcount it began the year with.
In a statement quoted by CTech, ServiceNow said: "We are making necessary changes to how we are structured. We are driving efficiencies across the business, actively investing in and hiring for AI-focused skills, and managing headcount with discipline to end 2026 where we started, as we shared earlier this year. That's how we grow sustainably and win."
Severance costs reflect the scale of workforce changes
ServiceNow's latest quarterly filing provides an indication of the financial impact of its ongoing workforce restructuring. The company reported higher employee severance and related costs during the first nine months of 2026 compared with the corresponding period last year.
Key figures from the filing include:
- $87 million in employee severance and related costs during the third quarter of 2026, compared with $24 million a year earlier.
- $167 million in severance and related costs during the first nine months of 2026, against $53 million in the same period last year.
- $153 million in cash payments towards severance during the first nine months of 2026.
- $34 million in severance-related reserves as of 30 September 2026.
The filing describes the programme as an effort to optimise the workforce through AI-driven efficiencies and investment in talent across strategic areas. ServiceNow expects the programme to be substantially completed during 2026.
The company recognises termination costs when employees receive notification, according to its filing. Consequently, costs associated with notifications from the latest round would normally be reflected in its fourth-quarter results.
AI efficiencies reshape workforce priorities
ServiceNow's leadership has previously discussed the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and employee numbers. During the company's third-quarter earnings call, CEO Bill McDermott described a smaller workforce as a "gorgeous situation" and said headcount had "slightly declined".
CFO Gina Mastantuono also said sales operations headcount was "down significantly", while the number of quota-carrying salespeople had increased by double digits.
She linked the slower pace of hiring to productivity improvements from AI. ServiceNow has said these efficiencies generate more than $1 billion in annualised gains.
The company's approach reflects a shift in workforce allocation, with greater emphasis on AI-focused roles and selected strategic capabilities. However, the latest announcement does not specify which functions or employee categories have been affected across India, the UK and the US.
Share decline adds pressure amid restructuring
The layoffs come during a period of weakness in ServiceNow's stock performance. According to CTech, the company's shares have fallen more than 30% since the beginning of 2026.
The stock also declined 35% between 23 October and 5 November, including a fall of approximately 27% the day after its third-quarter results.
ServiceNow had forecast fourth-quarter constant-currency current remaining performance obligations growth of 18.5%, below analysts' expectation of 19.8%, CTech reported.
The company had already undertaken workforce reductions earlier in the year. In July, layoffs affected hundreds of employees, including staff in Israel, with ServiceNow reiterating its intention to finish 2026 at its starting headcount.
The latest round signals the continuation of this restructuring programme. The number of affected employees and the precise impact across individual markets remain undisclosed, while the company continues to prioritise AI investment and operational efficiencies.

other-interests-0da0cf05b7.fulltext:
Laboratory robots are tireless and uncomplaining, but they have narrow skill sets, limited mobility and an inability to get out of each other’s way. Now, a system of artificial-intelligence agents promises to help lab robots do their best work.
In this process, a scientist describes their research programme and lab set-up to the agents, which then create step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The agents also generate a virtual version of the lab and test the protocols there. They can then direct the robots in the real lab to perform the research.
Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials
The agents can even design an entire lab from scratch, using a virtual one to work out the ideal placement for instruments and robots.
The system is described in a preprint posted in October to arXiv1. It has not been peer reviewed.
In a test, the agents wrote more than 200 commands directing a robotic arm to move between and interact with instruments in an existing lab space. The agent simulated the steps in the virtual lab to ensure that it all worked smoothly, then directed the real-life arm to carry out procedures to measure the optical properties of nanocrystals.
The concept is “very cool” and could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says Evan Collins, a bioengineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. But integrating the cameras and sensors that the agents need to direct experiments effectively could require more resources than does setting up a lab manually, he says.
Collision avoidance
The simulations would make it easy to plan robotic movements that avoid collisions between robots and other objects in the lab, says Collins.
This could ease the process of getting labs up and running, given that setting up an automated lab is often a time-consuming process of trial and error followed by extensive testing and troubleshooting. Because the agents conduct all the planning and testing in a simulated environment, there is no need for researchers to “babysit the system” after it’s built, says Yuchi (Allan) Zhao, a roboticist at the University of Toronto in Canada and co-author of the preprint.

other-interests-8f6b8825c3.headline: An unexpected feedback loop may be driving mega heatwaves
other-interests-8f6b8825c3.fulltext:
Mid-latitude regions such as Europe are set to suffer more intense heatwaves than previously thought, according to new research that has uncovered a three-way feedback loop that amplifies extreme heat conditions.
Heatwaves across the world have shocked scientists with their scale and severity in recent years, with heat extremes dramatically outstripping both historical records and the predictions of climate models.
In the UK in 2022, temperatures exceeded 40°C (104°F) for the first time in history, despite predictions that such a milestone was probably still years away. Likewise, the 2021 heatwave in the Pacific Northwest saw temperatures hit extremes that far outstripped climate model projections.
Advertisement
Researchers have been scrambling to understand why very extreme heat is occurring more frequently, and with greater intensity, than expected at this level of warming.
One team thinks the answer lies partly in the soil. Scientists already knew that high-pressure systems allow more solar radiation to reach Earth’s surface, heating up the land. They also knew that higher temperatures dry soils more quickly, removing the cooling effect provided by evaporation, thereby further amplifying heatwaves.
Now it seems that when temperatures climb high enough, dry soil, high pressure and extreme heat can amplify each other further, with dry soil helping to sustain high-pressure systems in the atmosphere.
“Basically, the soils that are affected by circulation pattern also start to affect back on the circulation pattern itself,” says Kai Kornhuber at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria.
This three-way feedback effect makes extreme heatwaves 10 per cent hotter than they would otherwise be, according to the research by Kornhuber and his colleagues – a factor not fully accounted for in climate model projections.
This will have serious consequences for our ability to cope with future extreme heat. “Ten per cent hotter or colder can really make a difference between a heatwave and a record-shattering heatwave,” says Kornhuber. “We’re facing so many critical thresholds in social and biophysical systems that an extra 10 per cent can really lead to temperatures that are then quite damaging.”
This may include serious public health consequences, a breakdown of vital infrastructure such as transport links and energy grids, crop failures and the collapse of ecosystems.
As the world warms due to climate change, regions including Europe, Russia, North America, parts of South America and Australia will hit thresholds where this feedback effect is triggered increasingly often. Kornhuber says work is now needed to ensure climate models are properly including this feedback effect when projecting future extremes.
Dim Coumou at the Free University of Amsterdam says the work helps to solve “part of the puzzle” of why heatwaves are outstripping model projections in their severity. “It shows that climate models are not doing a good job in reproducing this feedback mechanism, and that is a concern,” he says.
Governments should urgently start to prepare for more extreme heat events, he adds: “A region like Europe has to prepare for more intense heatwaves in the coming decades.”

longform-31049809d2.headline: Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?
longform-31049809d2.fulltext:
On 5 August 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost €250,000 (about £210,000 at the time), money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands.
To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. But that didn’t have to mean a mass recalibration of our consumption habits or a global shift away from red meat. Post and his team had found another way.
Standing at a blond-wood island on an otherwise empty soundstage, Post lifted the kind of stainless-steel cloche usually found on a room service cart to reveal his creation. The raw patty sat in a petri dish on a bare plate, where it shone wetly under the studio lights. With the ITV London anchor Nina Hossain presiding, a Cornish chef named Richard McGeown pan-fried the burger in sunflower oil and butter for two volunteer tasters: Josh Schonwald, the Chicago-based author of The Taste of Tomorrow: Dispatches from the Future of Food, and Hanni Rützler, an Austrian nutrition scientist. So precious was this meat that they were given just the one burger to share between them. It was served deconstructed, alongside a sesame-seed bun, lettuce and tomato – showmanship to sell the burger a bit, give it context. The patty itself was reddish brown, flat and perfectly circular. When Schonwald and Rützler cut it, the burger did not bleed.
The two of them ate with forks and knives, passing the plate, sawing off thoughtful bites. Chewing slowly. Afterwards, they rendered their verdicts. “I would say it is somewhere on the spectrum between a Boca Burger and McDonald’s,” Schonwald told a reporter from NBC. “The absence of fat makes a big difference. It has the texture, which I was not expecting. It was like an animal-protein cake.” Rützler noted the burger’s blandness to a reporter from Science. “There is room for improvement here,” she said. At the end of the event, about €113,000 worth of burger remained uneaten. But none of this stopped Post from predicting that meat cultivated in a lab would become a consumer product within the decade.
The event – the theatrical reveal, the PR spectacle – triggered a kind of gold rush. One hundred and forty companies sprang up in six continents, trying to replicate what Post had done with beef across a range of other species: chicken, pork, fish, even quail. Investment to the tune of $3bn (£2.2bn) flooded into the sector. True believers claimed that cellular agriculture would not only fight the climate crisis and global food insecurity but also slow the spread of zoonotic disease and antibiotic resistance. A company called Upside Foods touted its plans to “set the new standard for meat” and to “make meat a force of good in the world”. A company called Vow created an enormous woolly mammoth meatball, though no one was allowed to eat it, since the DNA came from a fossil and the company didn’t know whether it was actually fit for human consumption. The thinktank RethinkX predicted that cultivated meat would decimate the US beef industry by 2030, reducing demand for the conventional variety by a whopping 70%. As the organisation wrote, “We are already on the cusp of the deepest, fastest, most consequential disruption in food and agricultural production since the first domestication of plants and animals 10,000 years ago.”
And yet, despite the frenzy, the meat itself never arrived. The challenges were numerous. There was the exorbitant upfront cost of building manufacturing facilities and the daunting amounts of energy required to run them. There was the difficulty of producing sufficient quantities of the stuff, at a price point low enough for people to buy. There was the lack of a highly skilled workforce trained to operate the new technology. There were rounds and rounds of inspections by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). There was even, occasionally, the unwanted appearance of rodent DNA in research samples, which happened to the companies Upside and Eat Just. After peaking in 2021, investment began to fall off. In 2023, the industry raised a measly $177m globally.
But it wasn’t only venture capitalists who had started to grow sceptical of cultivated meat. The technology soon became a target of conservatives. The state governments of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Indiana, Montana, Nebraska and Texas moved in quick succession to legislate against cultivated meat, passing laws that banned its sale, production, or both. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis made a media event out of signing that state’s law, posing for pictures in front of a blood-stained cutting board piled high with steaks. “Take your fake lab-grown meat elsewhere,” he said. “We’re not doing that in the state of Florida.” In 2024, the industrial biotech consultant Joel Stone told the New York Times that, if he had to put odds on it, the likelihood of the industry producing even 10% of the meat supply in the foreseeable future “would be zero”. Today, cultivated meat is available for purchase at just one store in the world: Huber’s Butchery in Singapore, where customers can buy packages of lab-grown chicken shreds from a manufacturer called GOOD Meat.
These developments were inconvenient for me, a person who became obsessed with the prospect of tasting cell-grown meat just as the possibility of ever doing so seemed to recede before my eyes. I was enthralled by the story of the meat, which seemed to contain so much of what defined this era of American life: dubious techno-optimism, bombastic culture-war posturing, carnival oddities like the mammoth meatball. It presented a snarl of competing motives, a mix of altruism and cold-blooded striving for capital (nothing can ever exist just for the common good; it has to make someone a billionaire). There was also the fact that I had been a vegetarian for almost 20 years.
The last meat I ever ate was a hotdog at Shea Stadium in New York in 2007. I don’t remember how it tasted – probably like every other hotdog I had eaten before. I washed it down with an exorbitantly priced but very cold Budweiser in one of those metal bottles. I quit eating meat after that, not because the hotdog had been disgusting but because I didn’t like the sensation of the inevitable bad bite, the periodic tangle with gristle or tendon or bone. Then my abstention grew into habit, and the habit was reinforced by other concerns: the catastrophic environmental consequences of industrial meat production; the creeping doubt, as I grow older, that I’m necessarily higher in the cosmic order than a chicken or a cow. But cultivated meat raised a compelling question. If you could subtract some of the downsides – make meat less destructive, engineer away its aesthetic flaws – what reason would there be not to eat it?
This question had begun to feel moot as the potential of cultivated meat grew less and less promising. But just when it seemed as though Post’s vision would never be realised, encouraging news emerged from a surprising place: North Carolina. In May 2024, when many of his peers were fleeing the sector, Jeff Bezos granted $30m through his Earth Fund to establish the Bezos Center for Sustainable Protein at North Carolina State University, an initiative dedicated to developing “dietary proteins that are environmentally friendly, healthy, tasty and affordable”. The donation cemented the state’s status as a new global centre of the cultivated-meat industry. The Bezos Center would join the North Carolina Biotechnology Center, an economic development organisation for the life sciences in Research Triangle Park.
On the commercial side of things, Believer Meats, an Israeli company producing cultivated chicken, had recently broken ground on a 200,000 sq ft manufacturing plant in Wilson, North Carolina. The plant would be the largest cultivated-meat facility in the world – capable, the company claimed, of producing 9.5m kilos of engineered chicken per year.
In September 2025, Believer received a “no questions” letter from the FDA, indicating that the agency did not encounter safety concerns in its inspection of the company’s products. “We are proud to be commercialising in this state, creating high-quality manufacturing jobs and enabling us to realise our vision to lead food innovations that care for the planet,” said Believer’s then CEO, a man named (for real) Gustavo Burger, in a press release celebrating the milestone. I got in touch with the company shortly after. In a Zoom meeting with Heather Hudson, Believer’s chief product and growth officer, and Rodrigo Lavall, from sales and marketing, the two dangled the possibility of a ribbon-cutting ceremony. They could tentatively plan something and invite me down to visit.
The whole thing felt a bit Wonka-ish. No one from the press had been allowed inside the factory yet. Only a few professionals in the field had even toured it. Why should I get the golden ticket? But I tried not to question my good fortune. Excited by the prospect of exclusive access, I started planning a trip to the Triangle. If lab-grown meat had a future, I might find it there. Maybe, I thought, I’d even get to taste it.
On a mild day in early December, I arrived at NC State’s sprawling campus, home to about 40,000 students. I expected it to be lively, teeming with kids, but it was eerily dead. Rohan Shirwaiker, the friendly, bespectacled director of the Bezos Center, met me in a pristine building where I didn’t see a single student. Everyone, he explained, had gone home for the holidays.
The Bezos Center aims to address, as its website puts it, the “critical barriers and gaps” still dogging cultivated meat. The process has changed as the industry scales up. It’s no longer Post labouring over a single burger in his lab for years at a time. Cultivation now takes place in sterile factories that look more like breweries, with cells grown not in culture dishes but in giant, stainless-steel bioreactors. Producers have also moved away from feeding the cells with foetal bovine serum, which is expensive and requires harvesting cow blood from slaughterhouses (not exactly a good look for a cruelty-free alternative meat product). The industry now relies on what is referred to as “serum-free media”, or SFM, proprietary compounds that vary from company to company. Still, the basic science remains the same: in one typical version of the process, stem cells are harvested from a living animal via needle biopsy, then nourished in solutions containing glucose, vitamins, fats, minerals, proteins and amino acids, which are swished around inside a reactor to ensure an even diffusion of nutrients. In these conditions, the cells divide, multiply and differentiate just as they would inside an animal. They are ready for harvesting when they reach the desired density: roughly within two to eight weeks, depending on the species being cultivated.

OpenAI has closed on new funding of roughly $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, according to people familiar with the matter.
The funding was wired to the company as of Friday, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The remainder of the round, which could increase to as much as $20 billion in total, is expected to be completed in the coming weeks, one person said.
The AI developer has been in talks for more than a month to raise a large funding round after delaying its plans for an initial public offering. OpenAI initially set out to raise $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation, Bloomberg News has reported, before scaling back its plans amid a public market rout for the AI sector.
OpenAI declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal previously reported some details of the funding.
Investors that contributed to the first funding close include Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price, the people said. Other investors in the round include SoftBank Group Corp., Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz, people said. A syndicate of backers from the United Arab Emirates also joined, Bloomberg News has reported.

Softbank, Founders Fund and T. Rowe Price declined to comment. Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
The reduced funding goals represent a stark shift for a fundraising juggernaut that helped usher in the current AI boom. The sentiment around AI has also changed dramatically since the round kicked off, due to concerns about the spending spree on physical infrastructure for artificial intelligence and the potential for new roadblocks to data center construction following the US midterm elections.
Prospective investors in OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC’s upcoming IPO are also rethinking the Claude maker’s valuation. Potential buyers are discussing about a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion valuation range for Anthropic, Bloomberg News has reported, down from $1.5 trillion previously.

global-economics-cc779f2d59.headline: RBI meets bankers amidst rising AI cyber-attacks, mandates security audits
global-economics-cc779f2d59.fulltext:
Amidst the rising AI-assisted cyberattacks, especially on the financial sector, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), India’s central bank and main regulator for the banking sector, has possibly for the first time met bankers to address this issue since Cert-In started publishing advisories regarding the vulnerabilities reported.
According to an exclusive report by Head and Tale’s Arti Singh, the RBI reportedly held a nearly two-hour meeting with banks on Wednesday and issued a “confidential advisory” dated November 3. The banker told the reporter that the regulator “gave banks a dressing down” and stressed that banks are responsible for securing these arrangements. The banker also stated that individual frauds ranged from Rs. 3 crore to Rs. 15 crore, adding that the number of cyberattack attempts worried banks more.
The confidential RBI advisory reportedly also asked NBFCs which use APIs for a security audit by CERT-In empaneled auditor. These are the independent auditing companies which are approved by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). A full list of cybersecurity organizations which are listed on CERT-In’s website can be accessed here.
CERT-In names a threat actor: CERT-In’s November 4 advisory named a threat actor, “CRAFTY FALCON”. It said attackers used Rs. 1 transfers to test fund flows before larger transactions. It also said they bypassed IP allow-listing by routing traffic through shared third-party IP pools. CERT-In recommended beneficiary cooling periods and maker-checker approval for merchant settlements. Similarly, CERT-In has issued similar notices, you can find them here and here.
The next day, after the RBI meeting on November 3, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), which works under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), issued a public advisory on AI-assisted attacks on banks, NBFCs and fintechs. Both concern the application programming interfaces (APIs) that lenders use to disburse money.
Similarly, on the same day, CERT-In released AI Security Auditing Guidelines. Read MediaNama’s lowdown of the guidelines here.
Maintain a full API client inventory. The regulator has asked banks to capture business profile, services used, account and integration details, transaction limits, and key business, technical and security contacts.
Require CERT-In audits for NBFC clients. RBI has said the audit must be completed before onboarding new NBFCs, while existing clients have until February 3, 2027.
Conduct audits at least once a year. The regulator has reportedly asked banks to repeat the audit after any material cyber incident and to track completion and act on non-compliance.
Risk-assess non-NBFC API clients immediately. RBI also asked banks to require a periodic audit within three months for BCs, PAs, PSPs and fintechs, sooner if risk is higher.
Brief all API clients every three months on the current threat landscape, as per the regulator’s advisory.
Bring API transactions under fraud-risk and monitoring frameworks. The regulator has asked banks to set thresholds and behavioural baselines per client.
Flag material deviations. RBI has said banks must watch for volume or value spikes, transactions just below limits, odd-hour or holiday activity, bursts of new beneficiaries, mule patterns, failed log-ins and invalid API requests.
Monitor changes in apps. The regulator has asked banks to watch for changes in user-agent, app version, OS and network attributes, with technical changes due by December 3.
Secure banks’ own API infrastructure. The regulator has said banks must cover access management, network segmentation, patching and monitoring, as attackers may pivot through a compromised client.
Enforce beneficiary whitelisting. RBI has also asked banks to pre-register verified end-customer accounts per client, reject unregistered payouts, and allow additions or modifications only via a separate MFA-protected channel.
Enforce maker-checker or out-of-band confirmation. The regulator has said banks must add extra authorisation for API debit requests via a separate channel, applying it to all transactions or those above a risk-based threshold.
Require at least one safeguard from regulated entities using API-based fund transfers. The regulator has said new integrations must comply before they go-live, while existing ones have time until December 3, 2026.
Make debit information available quickly so clients can reconcile transactions one by one, as per the regulator’s direction.
Allow narrow, case-by-case exceptions only for highly automated payments where neither control is practical. The regulator has said a written application and documented risk assessment are required.
Set per-transaction and daily cumulative limits effective immediately. The regulator has asked banks to calibrate them to declare and observe business profile and risk.
Implement intra-day or velocity limits within one month to prevent bursts of transactions. RBI has said material limit increases need a documented risk assessment.
Treat maker-checker as a compensating safeguard for intra-day limits if commensurate with risk and documented, as the regulator has allowed.
Enforce immediate incident reporting and recovery. It has asked banks to ensure clients promptly report any actual or suspected compromise of systems connected to API-based payments.
CERT-In Director General Dr Sanjay Bahl, in written answers to MediaNama on November 2 and 3, described what worries the agency. He said that “delegated authority without commensurate guardrails and that AI agents are being trusted faster than they are being secured” concerns India’s nodal cyber security agency.
Note: MediaNama’s interview predates the RBI’s confidential advisory becoming public. Read the full interview here.
“What would change is the speed, scale and level of automation at which cyber activities take place. Defensive capabilities would therefore need to evolve accordingly from human-speed monitoring and manual containment to continuous, automated machine-speed defence.” – CERT-In Director General, Dr Sanjay Bahl.
AU Small Finance Bank is probing a “potential data leak” on a Salesforce-hosted platform after hackers claimed a breach. The bank says its systems are unaffected.
CoinDCX first dismissed reports of a breach, then confirmed a loss of about Rs. 152 crore.
Central Bank of India alleges hackers siphoned off Rs. 13.97 crore through its financial messaging system. It says it could not trace 187 transfers.
SBI confirmed a suspected breach of 3,897 customer records. Later they revealed that the customers have been informed through email and/or WhatsApp.
CBFC reportedly exposed scripts, distribution deals and censorship records for over 500 films. The board says it found no trace of the documents.
Amagi Media Labs faced an extortion attempt from a hacker claiming to hold operational and network data.
eMudhra is exiting the SSL/TLS certificate business days after researchers exposed weak private keys in eight intermediate certificates.
Railway, a cloud hosting platform, asked users to replace API keys after a cyberattack potentially exposed customer secrets.
CERT-In disclosed that AI agents accessed live Indian systems without authorisation during research and evaluation.
Anthropic said its Claude model found vulnerabilities across five targets, including Chrome, Android, Windows and Linux. It has not disclosed its success rate or computing costs.

However, the robotic capture petals did not deploy as planned, providing the company with data for further development.

The company estimates that its approach could bring satellite servicing costs down from around $10 million to below $1 million per satellite.
Cosmoserve plans to test its robotic capture systems through microgravity flights, reflight Mission Embrace and conduct a full-scale space debris capture demonstration in 2027.
The startup is among a growing number of Indian spacetech companies working on technologies spanning launch vehicles, satellite manufacturing, space data and orbital infrastructure. Hyderabad has also emerged as a spacetech hub, supported by its aerospace and defence ecosystem, engineering talent and research infrastructure.

indian-startups-e64b6c0d78.headline: MakeMyTrip acquires majority stake in Quick Ride to enter shared mobility segment
indian-startups-e64b6c0d78.fulltext:
Travel technology platform MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake in Bengaluru-based shared mobility startup Quick Ride, marking its entry into the ride pooling segment. The acquisition will expand MakeMyTrip’s ground transportation portfolio and strengthen its presence in daily urban commutes.
Entrackr exclusively reported on October 19 that MakeMyTrip was in talks to acquire Quick Ride through its subsidiary redBus. However, the financial details of the transaction have not been disclosed.
Founded in 2015 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride is an asset-light mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes for car and bike pooling. It enables users to share rides for everyday commutes and offers services to corporate employees through partnerships with companies, IT parks and business campuses. The platform aims to make commuting more affordable while reducing the number of vehicles on roads.
According to MakeMyTrip, Quick Ride’s ride pooling business and brand have undergone an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the brand and its ride pooling business through a majority stake in this entity. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business, while its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited.
Commenting on the development, Rajesh Magow, Co-founder and Group CEO of MakeMyTrip, said the acquisition will help the company establish a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, alongside intercity travel. He added that Quick Ride will be housed under MakeMyTrip’s ground transport business, which will leverage its experience in building redBus in India and overseas markets to scale the platform.
Prakash Sangam, CEO of redBus and Head of Ground Transport at MakeMyTrip, said the acquisition will expand the company’s offerings across different travel needs. The platform sees an opportunity to serve the same customers across their daily office commutes and intercity journeys.
Quick Ride has raised funding from investors including Sequoia Capital India (now Peak XV Partners), Naspers (now part of Prosus) and Venture Highway. In 2019, the company raised Rs 100.78 crore ($14.4 million) in a Series B round from its existing investors.
The acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip’s strategy to expand its presence across travel segments through acquisitions and strategic investments. In recent years, the company has acquired Savaari in the car rental segment, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys.
The latest acquisition adds ride pooling to its ground transportation portfolio, which already includes redBus and Savaari. The company said the addition of Quick Ride will help it offer customers a wider range of travel options, from daily commutes to intercity journeys.

More than $1.2 billion in capital announced in 2026 powers strategic acquisitions, on-orbit operations, next-generation space infrastructure, and global expansion.
CesiumAstro Inc., a global leader in space and defense communications systems and satellites, today announced the closing of $730 million in Series D financing, valuing the company at more than $4.5 billion. The financing brings CesiumAstro’s total capital announced in 2026 to more than $1.2 billion and supports its expansion into developing and operating its own satellite infrastructure.
The company also announced Synchronicity, a planned 737-satellite, AI-enabled constellation for commercial, sovereign, and defense missions. The announcement follows the launch of CesiumAstro’s first satellite Element-1, and the start of its on-orbit operations.
This expansion builds on three strategic acquisitions that have strengthened CesiumAstro’s vertical integration from semiconductors to mission operations, helping accelerate the development and deployment of Synchronicity. The company is also expanding its engineering and manufacturing operations worldwide. As part of that effort, CesiumAstro has announced a $500 million investment over five years to expand its Austin-area headquarters, including the purchase of 270,000 square feet of advanced manufacturing space.
The equity round was led by Janus Henderson, with participation from Insight Partners, Sands Capital, Sumitomo Corporation of Americas, Woven Capital – Toyota’s Growth Fund, Incharge Capital, Magnetar, AV, and NewSpace Capital, alongside $100 million in debt financing provided through the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and JPMorgan.
The new capital will support advanced technologies, expansion of U.S. manufacturing capacity, development and production of next-generation spacecraft, Synchronicity deployment, and international growth.
“For nearly a decade, we have invested in the engineering, intellectual property, manufacturing infrastructure, and the talented people required to build an enduring space technology company,” said Shey Sabripour, Founder and CEO of CesiumAstro. “With our technology proven on orbit, on the ground and in the air, a significantly expanded set of capabilities, and more than $1.2 billion in new capital raised this year, we are positioned to take the next major step in our growth.”
“Shey Sabripour is an extraordinary entrepreneur, and CesiumAstro is poised to revolutionize the space communications industry. This industry is at an inflection point; legacy solutions are not equipped for the demands of today’s customers,” said Aaron Schaechterle, Portfolio Manager, Janus Henderson. “When we met Shey and his team, it became clear that CesiumAstro provides transformative technology that is critical to the industry’s future. This investment was originated through the Janus Henderson Ascent platform, which was created to provide private market capital to visionary companies that redefine their industries and to support these companies on the journey from private to public markets.”
Synchronicity takes CesiumAstro beyond supplying advanced space technologies and complete spacecraft to developing and operating its own integrated space infrastructure.
The constellation is designed around a dynamically managed, multi-beam, multi-frequency architecture supporting Ku-, Ka-, and V-band communications, advanced edge compute, and multi-orbit operations. This unified system aims to deliver more flexible, resilient, and adaptable connectivity across a broad range of commercial and national security missions.
AI is integrated throughout the architecture, enabling network optimization, dynamic allocation of communications resources, and autonomous adaptation to changing mission requirements and operating conditions. Edge processing capabilities are intended to bring compute closer to where data is generated, reducing dependence on terrestrial infrastructure and supporting increasingly time-sensitive applications.
Unlike architectures assembled from independently sourced components, Synchronicity will leverage CesiumAstro’s vertically integrated technology portfolio, including custom silicon, best-in-class active phased arrays, software-defined payloads, advanced processors, spacecraft, mission software, and terminals for air, ground, mobility, and maritime platforms. This approach enables system-wide performance optimization.
“Synchronicity is the culmination of the technology stack we have methodically built since CesiumAstro was founded,” said Sabripour. “We designed the silicon, the active phased array, the payload, processors, the spacecraft, ground terminals, and the network as one system. That vertical integration gives us the ability to build capabilities in space that evolve as mission requirements, technology, and operating conditions change.”
In the past 12 months, CesiumAstro has brought critical semiconductor, mission software, and artificial intelligence capabilities together through three acquisitions: Jariet Technologies, 1Aardvark, and Vidrovr.
Jariet Technologies — A leading millimeter-wave RF System-on-Chip (RF-SoC) semiconductor company specializing in advanced solutions for satellite communications, electronic warfare, and radar systems. The acquisition strengthens CesiumAstro’s technology portfolio with advanced mixed-signal semiconductors, digital signal processing, and digital beamforming capabilities, enabling greater performance and control across its communications payloads, active phased arrays, and spacecraft.
1Aardvark — A company specializing in mission software, algorithms, and systems engineering for national defense programs. The acquisition expands CesiumAstro’s autonomous mission capabilities, enabling spacecraft to dynamically respond to changing conditions, operate with greater resilience, and maintain mission effectiveness in contested or connectivity-constrained environments.
Vidrovr — An AI company specializing in real-time multimodal signal analysis. The acquisition accelerates CesiumAstro’s integration of AI into space communications and sensing systems, enabling intelligent RF optimization, autonomous satellite operations, and reconfigurable edge compute across its space and defense platforms.
CesiumAstro successfully launched and began on-orbit operation of Element-1 in October 2026.
Element-1 integrates CesiumAstro’s proprietary communications payloads, active phased array technology, compute systems, and spacecraft engineering in an operational satellite. The mission validates nearly a decade of investment in proprietary intellectual property, specialized engineering expertise, and in-house manufacturing capabilities.
Element-1 is the first of eight planned spacecraft, with seven more launches secured for the next deployment phase. The Element program also advances CesiumAstro’s space-based edge processing and compute capabilities, enabling data to be processed closer to its source and supporting more intelligent, responsive, and autonomous missions.
In Texas, CesiumAstro announced a $500 million investment over five years to expand its global headquarters in Austin, including the purchase of 270,000 square feet of advanced manufacturing space. The expansion will support precision electronics and spacecraft manufacturing, engineering, integration, and test, with plans to add 550 jobs and grow the Austin-area workforce to more than 1,000 employees by 2030.
Across the United States, the company is investing hundreds of millions of dollars to expand its engineering, manufacturing, and operational capabilities, with additional facilities in Colorado, California, Alabama, Florida, and the Washington, D.C. area.
In Europe and Asia, the company is expanding its presence, with operations in the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, Taiwan, Singapore, and Japan.
These expansions will support scaled production of its communications and sensing systems, advanced compute technologies, and spacecraft, as well as development and deployment of its next-generation space infrastructure.

After the Republicans suffered a devastating defeat in the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that his Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles, will step down and her deputy, Stephen Miller, will take her place.

She has done a great job," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Wiles also posted a statement shortly after the announcement. "Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff. Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime. world-583af74911.headline: Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
world-583af74911.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
world-583af74911.fulltext:
Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
Miller has been a close confidant of Trump since 2016 and an architect of the president’s hardline immigration policies.
United States President Donald Trump has tapped his longtime adviser Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff.
The move on Friday represented a doubling down on Trump’s most controversial policies following his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing earlier this week.
Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January, and are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller’s role in the White House.
The 41-year-old Miller has been one of Trump’s most vocal defenders and is widely seen as an architect of the president’s mass deportation campaign.
In his post on Truth Social, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors”, saying he would take over the role from Susie Wiles on Monday.
An early adherent
Miller had built a reputation as a conservative activist long before entering Trump’s orbit.
At Santa Monica High School, he cut his teeth railing against what he described as liberal school policies on local radio shows.
At Duke University, he led the Duke Conservative Union and became a staunch advocate for three of the school’s lacrosse players after they were accused of rape.
After college, he moved to Washington, DC, where he worked as a legislative aide to Republican members of Congress and Republican Senator Jeff Sessions.
He joined Trump’s initial presidential campaign in January 2016, where he was credited with shaping the president’s messaging and caustic political stylings.
“I think he and Trump hit it off from the very beginning,” former Trump adviser Steve Bannon told The Associated Press news agency in 2017. “I think he helped Trump find his voice.”
What was his role during Trump’s first term?
Following Trump’s surprise victory in the 2016 race, Miller assumed the role of presidential adviser and speechwriter.
He served as an influential voice in shaping Trump’s most strident actions related to immigration, often framing the issues as an effort to protect Western “civilisation”.
During that period, Democratic lawmakers accused Miller of perpetuating white nationalist rhetoric.
In 2019, the Southern Poverty Law Center released emails allegedly showing the Trump adviser supporting white nationalist websites and ideologies. That spurred a renewed push from Democratic lawmakers, who sought Miller’s removal from the White House.
“It is unacceptable for the Trump Administration to knowingly install a known white nationalist and believer of white supremacist ideology in a position of power and influence over federal policy,” Congress member Joaquin Castro said in a statement in 2020.
Miller is credited with shaping the Department of Justice’s 2018 “Zero Tolerance” policy at the US border, which called for the arrest of nearly every adult crossing into the US without legal documentation.
The scheme resulted in widespread family separation, with children barred from being housed in criminal detention facilities along with their parents. Trump later changed the policy via executive order, amid widespread outrage.
As an adviser to Trump, Miller campaigned to end Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), a programme that allowed individuals brought to the US as children without documentation to receive legal paperwork for education and employment. The programme stopped accepting new applicants in 2021.
Miller also drove wide-scale visa restrictions during Trump’s first term, including a 2017 travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, which came to be known as the “Muslim travel ban”.
The initial order blocked citizens of Syria, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen from entering the US for 90 days. An adjusted version of the policy was eventually upheld by the US Supreme Court.
He later became a top proponent of Trump’s unfounded claims that the 2020 election was stolen, supporting a scheme for Trump to be certified as the victor.
Trump 2.0
Miller remained by Trump’s side as the former president staged a political comeback ahead of the 2024 presidential vote. He became Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser when the administration retook office in January 2025.
Since then, he has helped to orchestrate Trump’s mass deportation drive, which has seen immigration enforcement agents flood communities across the country, increasingly targeting individuals with no or only minor criminal records.
In May 2025, Miller told Fox News the administration had “set a goal of a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day, and President Trump is going to keep pushing to get that number up higher each and every day”.
He has also been a vocal defender of increasingly violent tactics by immigration agents. He initially defended the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during an operation in Minneapolis, calling them both “terrorists” before walking back the statement about Pretti.
As part of Trump’s deportation efforts, the administration has sought to expel visa-holders and permanent residents who have been supportive of Palestinian rights and critical of the Israeli government’s abuses in places like Gaza and the West Bank.
The Trump administration has argued that such views are harmful to US foreign policy. Miller’s role in that crafting that position has come under scrutiny in recent months.
In July, Mahmoud Khalil, a former graduate student at Columbia University, filed a lawsuit against several Trump administration officials, including Miller, accusing them of orchestrating “a conspiracy to single out Mr Khalil and other non-citizen Palestinians”.
Khalil continues to face deportation proceedings under Trump for his role in pro-Palestinian protests.
In the past, Miller has criticised pro-Palestinian voices, like that of US Representative Rashida Tlaib, considered the first Palestinian American woman to serve in Congress.
“Rashida Tlaib should be expelled from Congress,” Miller told Fox News in 2023, as he proceeded to call the representative and other Democrats “deeply anti-Semitic and deeply anti-American”.
In his return to the White House, Miller also unsuccessfully sought to end birthright citizenship, while becoming an increasingly vocal defender of Trump’s military actions in the Western Hemisphere.
He endorsed the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and told CNN in January that the US had a right to seize Greenland based on its military might.
“We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said.
“These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”
What does a chief of staff do?
It was not immediately clear how Miller’s new role would affect his influence over Trump.
The chief of staff is typically tasked with overseeing White House staff and hiring, maintaining the president’s calendar, and advising the president on policy.
Some insiders refer to the role, which largely controls information flows, as the “gatekeeper” to the presidency.
